LIFE-SAVING LYMPHOEDEMA SURGERY

By: Latashia Naidoo | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In a world first for South African medicine, one Cape Town vascular surgery is bringing long-term relief to sufferers of debilitating lymphoedema

Unique Selling Point:
It's the first surgery of its kind to be offered to sufferers of lymphoedema in South Africa. Lymphoedema is a notoriously debilitating progressive condition with currently no known cure that affects people dealing with cancer and HIV??


Summary:
Imagine beating all the odds and surviving cancer… just to be left with lingering, life and lifestyle-changing side effects which no one talks about. It’s known as “cancer’s dirty little secret”, a condition which can persist for life and leaves the patient with debilitating chronic pain.
Lymphoedema is a notoriously progressive condition with currently no known cure. The lymph node disorder results in blockages in the lymphatic system, which causes swelling of the extremities - and excruciating pain.
Now a life-altering procedure that brings relief to patients has been brought to South Africa by Cape Town-based vascular surgeon, Dr Laura Redman.
Dr Redman trained for this groundbreaking type of debulking surgery in Sweden and the first procedure in Africa was done in 2020.
The surgery can improve the quality of life for sufferers, without the potential of a recurrence.
It’s the first-of-its-kind to be done by an African doctor, because of how specialised the surgery is - only a handful of surgeons around the world are trained to perform this.

Further information:
It’s proven successful for 40-year-old Simone Blackenberg from Cape Town, the first patient to undergo this surgery in March 2020. Blanckenberg was living with lymphoedema for eight years before surgery.
Her condition was triggered when she gave birth to her son seven years ago, and her leg swelled up to 5 times its actual size.
Since the surgery, her leg has returned to its normal proportions, and she no longer has to endure chronic hip or back pain as a result of the condition - or undergo hip replacement surgery which she was advised of.
Alexis Yapp was diagnosed with Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma in 2004. She’s been suffering with lymphoedema in her right arm since 2005, which left her “disabled” on her right side.
She’s the latest patient to have the debulking surgery, and her life has changed monumentally since. She can once again do things like write and paint - which she lost the ability to do when she developed the condition.

Black women - particularly breast cancer survivors - are most likely to develop Lymphoedema, which is why this type of surgery is so important within South Africa.
Dr Redman has launched a programme to raise funds for at-risk patients living in rural communities, to assist them with funding for this life-changing treatment.

Web Contacts:

LAOSA is a South African non-profit (164-391 NPO) organisation for professional individuals interested in lymphoedema treatment, as well as research and training in lymphology and lymphoedema. We strive to promote access to complete Lymphoedema care in the public and private healthcare sectors. We provide the public, medical colleagues and third party payors with a National Practice Register of those qualified to treat Lymphoedema in order to ensure standards of care in the field of Lymphoedema are upheld. LAOSA engages regularly with Medical Aids and Third Party Payors to improve the reimbursement for treatment.

Press Release:


Cancer’s Dirty Secret
In 2013, Simone Blanckenberg was a dedicated runner and a new mom to a beautiful baby boy. She’d beaten cancer – twice – and was finally in remission. Then just three days after giving birth, her leg became excruciatingly painful, swelling to double its normal size. The diagnosis - a little known and debilitating condition called Lymphoedema - a remnant of the life-saving cancer surgery she’d undergone a few years before. Now an innovative operation which closely mimics the cosmetic procedure liposuction, is helping her live a full life again. Carte Blanche explores how this medical solution - a first for the continent - is changing the prognosis for lymphoedema patients.
Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


LYMPHOEDEMA - FINAL
Kian: I’d say constantly I have pain, but I’m used to it.”
VO:
16-year-old Kian January just wants to be a regular teenager. Football-mad, and a gamer…
VO:
… his life changed dramatically three years ago, when what he thought were growing pains from puberty - turned out to be something highly unusual.
CAM2 CARD1 AA873601 - 02:03 -
Masa: “ When you realised the swelling and the pain is getting increased, what did you think it was?”
Kian: “I thought because I was playing soccer it caused the pain or I injured myself while playing.
VO: Medical science has shown that Kian is one in one hundred thousand: he was born with a rare condition that causes extreme pain and swelling in his right leg.
VO: It’s called Lymphoedema…a chronic condition in which his limb swells up, because his body’s lymphatic system is blocked.
VO:
Imagine a drain pipe, which takes dirty dishwater out of a sink…
In a similar way, the lymphatic system filters harmful waste out of the body…without it toxins that build up in the body, can’t drain out.
MASA LINK: CAM1 50p CARD 1 A7s36276: “Lymphoedema usually affects the arm or the leg, but it can affect other parts of the body as well. The condition can cause long-term physical, psychological and social problems for patients.”
VO:
Kian’s condition - known as a vascular malformation - is a form of primary lymphoedema. The only way he can manage the swelling is by wearing specialised compression garments. And it’s not comfortable…
Kian experiences pain, and intense pins and needles sensations in his leg - constantly.
SHOWING THE COMPRESSION GARMENT:
MASA: “Are you wearing a compression garment?”
KIAN: “Yes.”
MASA: “What does it feel like wearing that?”
KIAN: “It helps with blood flow and the swelling. Also, it reduces it.”
VO:
For years, no one was able to help Kian with the debilitating pain.
That was until he met vascular surgeon Dr Laura Redman in 2020 - who has been something of a medical fairy Godmother for Kian and his family.
VIZ: Video of Dr Redman with Kian after surgery
VO:
Dr Redman is a super-specialist - as a surgeon she enjoyed the intricacies of the arteries, veins and vessels that carry blood through the body.
It’s taken 13 operations, but Dr Redman’s helped to manually reduce the swelling in Kian’s right leg to a point where he may still play football for Liverpool someday.
KIAN:
“I’m hoping that after all the operations – most of the ops, the big ops – physio-wise, getting back to walking without crutches, that I can play soccer again. I haven’t played in years.”
VO:
But there’s more to Lymphedema than just being a congenital condition.
For years it’s been called “cancer’s dirty little secret” - but it’s a secret that people fighting cancer are often the very last to hear about, and then only when parts of their bodies are already swelling up.
LAURA: “Lymphoedema is a collection of lymph fluid in a limb – particularly a leg or an arm – which can appear post-surgery, or as a congenital malformation, and the limb will swell.”
VO:
After beating cancer twice - a monumental accomplishment - Simone Blanckenburg gave birth to a baby boy in 2013. Soon after, she noticed some swelling in her leg.
SIMONE: “It was almost within two or three days, literally. The lymph fluid just started to pool in my leg.”
VO:
Just like that, Simone was initiated into the secret that affects millions of cancer survivors globally - secondary Lymphoedema the aftershock of cancer surgery.
SIMONE: I had no lymph glands to essentially move the lymphatic fluid out of my limb. And so it just sat there, and my limb literally almost doubled overnight.”
LAURA: “Anyone who has surgery of the lymph nodes in the armpit or the groin – so most of those surgeries are cancer surgeries, so can be lymphoma, or a gynecological cancer, prostate cancer – and then radiotherapy will additionally damage the lymphatics, and affect either the arm or the leg in that way.”
VO:
Explaining it may be simple, but the treatment is notoriously difficult.
Until now, patients faced a life of trying to relieve discomfort with exercise, compression garments, and specialised massages.
MASA LINK: “In the past, lymphoedema patients would have to wear something like this – a compression garment – which was the main way they could manage the condition. But thanks to a groundbreaking procedure called ‘debulking’, they can now live a somewhat normal life.”
VO:
After years of watching her Lymphoedema patients endure pain and suffering, Dr Redman decided it was time to find a solution.
In 2019, she travelled to Sweden to train with world-renowned Plastic and Reconstructive surgeon, Dr Hakan Brorson, who first patented a surgery called “debulking”.
On the face of it, debulking looks a bit like liposuction.
LAURA: “It’s a power-assisted liposuction but it’s not normal lipo because you’re not going in areas – it’s the entire limb and huge volumes, and he designed cannulas to remove this tissue.”
VO:
Dr Redman became the only specialist on the continent that can do debulking.
And she’s been changing lives ever since…
LAURA: “So the whole idea is to make the limb more functionable and the same size as the other, So we get the volume down, but because we can’t cure lymphoedema – so we haven’t fixed the underlying cause – to ensure it doesn’t recur they have to be in lifelong compression, day and night.”
VO:
In March 2020, Simone was the first patient in Africa to undergo the procedure.
LAURA: “So how are you doing Simone, after two years?”
SIMONE: “Ya. It’s been an amazing, life-changing procedure.”
VO:
Simone’s debulking surgery took seven-and-a-half hours. Dr Redman was able to remove 4 litres of fluid from her right leg.
SIMONE: “Within two weeks I was exercising again. Within three weeks I went and bought myself a whole new wardrobe.
VO:
In June 2021, Alexis Yapp became the second patient to undergo debulking. In remission for over a decade for Non Hodgkin’s lymphoma, Alexis awoke one day with her arm double its size.
ALEXIS: “I thought I’d been bitten by something - it was really hot and red and I thought I had an allergic reaction.”
VO:
But after a few days, her arm just got worse. And her lymphoedema - misdiagnosed repeatedly.
ALEXIS: “... nobody could tell me what it was at first… was never told about it by any of my oncologists or my doctors - this could be a side effect.”
VO:
Alexis has become something of a patient advocate to try and prevent the needless suffering she experienced by not understanding the condition.
ALEXIS: If you know about it you can be in the correct compression, you can see the correct physios, you can avoid stuff that makes the lymphoedema worse.”
VO:
Because lymphoedema is life-long, the financial burden can be as crippling as the physical. Simone fought with her medical aid for years to get them to cover her surgery and treatment costs.
MASA: “You were in pain, you were suffering, and the medical aid wasn’t understanding this at some point and seeing this procedure as cosmetic.”
SIMONE: “This wasn’t liposuction because I had some cellulite on my bum and I didn’t like it. Firstly it was related to cancer and secondly it was completely debilitating for me and was leading to huge long-term physical implications, and so getting them to understand that was quite something.”
VO:
Meanwhile, as doctors continue to search for a cure for Lymphoedema, Simone says that two years post-surgery, she’s feeling just swell - this time, for all the right reasons.
SIMONE: “Life is really dramatically different. From both a physical perspective, mental perspective, physiologically – it’s been a complete miracle, actually.”

____
PROMO 1:
VO:
While life-saving cancer treatments can be harsh on the body, they can also cause potential long-term side effects - that add to sufferers’ physical and emotional trauma.


PROMO 2:
VO:
It’s a breakthrough new surgery that spells hope for what many call cancer’s dirty little secret
LAURA: “It’s one thing to have survived cancer, but the impact of lymphoedema has a severe effect on quality of life. So when the limb gets huge, they get musculoskeletal problems, pain, infection - it’s a lot of problems with it.”

PROMO 2:
Masa: It’s a common side effect of cancer treatment that causes extreme pain and swelling in the legs and arms. Now, a first-for-Africa procedure is helping cancer survivors reclaim their quality of life.
SIMONE: “Major hip issues. I think that if I hadn’t have had the debulking operation, I would’ve landed up having to have a hip replacement – without a doubt.”

TUESDAY PROMO:
VO:
Imagine beating the odds and surviving cancer… just to be left with a chronic and debilitating side effect of limbs swelling up - for the rest of your life.

ALEXIS: “I thought I’d been bitten by something - it was really hot and red and I thought I had an allergic reaction.” VO: But after a few days, her arm just got worse. And her lymphoedema - misdiagnosed repeatedly. ALEXIS: “... nobody could tell me what it was at first… was never told about it by any of my oncologists or my doctors - this could be a side effect.” VO: Alexis has become something of a patient advocate to try and prevent the needless suffering she experienced by not understanding the condition. ALEXIS: If you know about it you can be in the correct compression, you can see the correct physios, you can avoid stuff that makes the lymphoedema worse.” VO: Because lymphoedema is life-long, the financial burden can be as crippling as the physical. Simone fought with her medical aid for years to get them to cover her surgery and treatment costs. MASA: “You were in pain, you were suffering, and the medical aid wasn’t understanding this at some point and seeing this procedure as cosmetic.” SIMONE: “This wasn’t liposuction because I had some cellulite on my bum and I didn’t like it. Firstly it was related to cancer and secondly it was completely debilitating for me and was leading to huge long-term physical implications, and so getting them to understand that was quite something.” VO: Meanwhile, as doctors continue to search for a cure for Lymphoedema, Simone says that two years post-surgery, she’s feeling just swell - this time, for all the right reasons. SIMONE: “Life is really dramatically different. From both a physical perspective, mental perspective, physiologically – it’s been a complete miracle, actually.” ____ PROMO 1: VO: While life-saving cancer treatments can be harsh on the body, they can also cause potential long-term side effects - that add to sufferers’ physical and emotional trauma. PROMO 2: VO: It’s a breakthrough new surgery that spells hope for what many call cancer’s dirty little secret LAURA: “It’s one thing to have survived cancer, but the impact of lymphoedema has a severe effect on quality of life. So when the limb gets huge, they get musculoskeletal problems, pain, infection - it’s a lot of problems with it.” PROMO 2: Masa: It’s a common side effect of cancer treatment that causes extreme pain and swelling in the legs and arms. Now, a first-for-Africa procedure is helping cancer survivors reclaim their quality of life. SIMONE: “Major hip issues. I think that if I hadn’t have had the debulking operation, I would’ve landed up having to have a hip replacement – without a doubt.” TUESDAY PROMO: VO: Imagine beating the odds and surviving cancer… just to be left with a chronic and debilitating side effect of limbs swelling up - for the rest of your life.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In a world first for South African medicine, one Cape Town vascular surgery is bringing long-term relief to sufferers of debilitating lymphoedema
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It's the first surgery of its kind to be offered to sufferers of lymphoedema in South Africa. Lymphoedema is a notoriously debilitating progressive condition with currently no known cure that affects people dealing with cancer and HIV??
metadata.Summary: Imagine beating all the odds and surviving cancer… just to be left with lingering, life and lifestyle-changing side effects which no one talks about. It’s known as “cancer’s dirty little secret”, a condition which can persist for life and leaves the patient with debilitating chronic pain. Lymphoedema is a notoriously progressive condition with currently no known cure. The lymph node disorder results in blockages in the lymphatic system, which causes swelling of the extremities - and excruciating pain. Now a life-altering procedure that brings relief to patients has been brought to South Africa by Cape Town-based vascular surgeon, Dr Laura Redman. Dr Redman trained for this groundbreaking type of debulking surgery in Sweden and the first procedure in Africa was done in 2020. The surgery can improve the quality of life for sufferers, without the potential of a recurrence. It’s the first-of-its-kind to be done by an African doctor, because of how specialised the surgery is - only a handful of surgeons around the world are trained to perform this.
metadata.Further information: It’s proven successful for 40-year-old Simone Blackenberg from Cape Town, the first patient to undergo this surgery in March 2020. Blanckenberg was living with lymphoedema for eight years before surgery. Her condition was triggered when she gave birth to her son seven years ago, and her leg swelled up to 5 times its actual size. Since the surgery, her leg has returned to its normal proportions, and she no longer has to endure chronic hip or back pain as a result of the condition - or undergo hip replacement surgery which she was advised of. Alexis Yapp was diagnosed with Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma in 2004. She’s been suffering with lymphoedema in her right arm since 2005, which left her “disabled” on her right side. She’s the latest patient to have the debulking surgery, and her life has changed monumentally since. She can once again do things like write and paint - which she lost the ability to do when she developed the condition. Black women - particularly breast cancer survivors - are most likely to develop Lymphoedema, which is why this type of surgery is so important within South Africa. Dr Redman has launched a programme to raise funds for at-risk patients living in rural communities, to assist them with funding for this life-changing treatment.
metadata.Web Contacts: https://www.laosa.co.za/ LAOSA is a South African non-profit (164-391 NPO) organisation for professional individuals interested in lymphoedema treatment, as well as research and training in lymphology and lymphoedema. We strive to promote access to complete Lymphoedema care in the public and private healthcare sectors. We provide the public, medical colleagues and third party payors with a National Practice Register of those qualified to treat Lymphoedema in order to ensure standards of care in the field of Lymphoedema are upheld. LAOSA engages regularly with Medical Aids and Third Party Payors to improve the reimbursement for treatment.
